case.question: Find advice about running customer interviews from guests other than Teresa Torres.
case.expected_behavior: Retrieve customer-research interview advice while respecting the Teresa Torres exclusion.
case.rubric: Use relevant non-Teresa advice; podcast-host interviews or job interviews alone do not satisfy customer interviews. Do not attribute excluded Teresa passages to another guest.

answer.summary: To run customer interviews, Zoelle Egner suggests writing a template email to send to customers, asking for their feedback and experience with the product, and setting aside time for unstructured conversations.

sections.heading: Zoelle Egner's advice on running customer interviews
sections.content: To run customer interviews, Zoelle Egner suggests writing a template email to send to customers, asking for their feedback and experience with the product, and setting aside time for unstructured conversations.

sections.heading: Lane Shackleton's advice on running customer interviews
sections.content: Lane Shackleton advises that knowing the customer is crucial, and it's essential to have good intuitions about where the customer's headed and what they want. He also mentions that it's easier than ever to get into the customer's mindset with the help of tools.

sections.heading: Dalton Caldwell's advice on running customer interviews
sections.content: Dalton Caldwell recommends getting out in the world and talking to people in person, rather than hiding behind a keyboard and calling it customer interaction. He also suggests setting aside 20-30% of your time for customer meetings and calls.

sections.heading: Paige Costello's advice on running customer interviews
sections.content: Paige Costello emphasizes the importance of customer centricity and suggests becoming best friends with a researcher to watch customers use the product firsthand. She also advises bringing insight to every meeting and being willing to ask great questions.

sections.heading: Oji Udezue's advice on running customer interviews
sections.content: Oji Udezue suggests organizing customer conversations so that PMs, designers, and engineers have them on their calendar every week. He also advises training them on how to have the conversation, as the death of customer discovery is friction.

sections.heading: Episode advice (speaker unidentified)
sections.content: An unidentified speaker advises finding participants who want to opt into research and building a database of customers who are aware of and expect to be contacted for research. They also suggest enabling user researchers to use this database to contact customers more effectively.

sections.heading: Gia Laudi's advice on running customer interviews
sections.content: Gia Laudi suggests working with SparkToro's best customers to learn from them and guide research. She also advises using surveys as a starting point and doubling down with interviews if needed.

S7.text:
king to customers, another one of your big bullet points in the book is around continuous customer discovery, and I'm curious what you found to be successful in actually doing that. A lot of people talk about it when you keep talking to customers, get feedback constantly. What actually works in your experience?

Oji Udezue (00:31:34):
Yeah, I feel like all of park management is about discovery these days. Everyone talks about it, and I want to make a distinction. I think discovery is when you use customer conversations to understand a very specific thing that you want to optimize further workflow that you want to optimize further. And then you call the people who are most likely to be affected and you do use various research strategies to talk to them. There's a version of that also that is what I call continuous conversations, which is a Calendly and a Typeform, which we'll do more and more of. You should organize it so that your PMs, your designers, your engineering managers and your PMMs are constantly talking to customers by default. Meaning that customer conversations show up on their calendar every week automagically, without them getting involved. And then they're trained on how to have the conversation, because the death of customer discovery is friction. If you ask individuals to do customer discovery, they will not do customer discovery.

answer.summary: To find customers, set up interviews consistently, and conduct them, Zoelle Egner recommends writing a template email for yourself that you can send out easily, thanking the recipient for using the product, and asking for their experience and feedback. She also suggests setting up a hypothesis of the type of person you want to talk to and running a query against your database to find someone to send three emails a week. Dalton Caldwell advises that overcoming social anxiety and awkwardness when talking to customers requires getting past the feeling of looking stupid and starting to do it until it doesn't feel bad anymore. He also suggests setting up a system to talk to customers, such as having 20-30% of your time dedicated to customer meetings, and that nothing substitutes for an actual conversation versus just staring at analytics dashboards.

sections.content: Dalton Caldwell recommends getting out in the world and talking to people in person, rather than hiding behind a keyboard and calling it customer interaction. He also suggests setting aside 20-30% of your time for customer meetings and calls.

sections.heading: Paige Costello's advice on running customer interviews
sections.content: Paige Costello emphasizes the importance of customer centricity and suggests becoming best friends with a researcher to watch customers use the product firsthand. She also advises bringing insight to every meeting and being willing to ask great questions.

sections.heading: Oji Udezue's advice on running customer interviews
sections.content: Oji Udezue suggests organizing customer conversations so that PMs, designers, and engineers have them on their calendar every week. He also advises training them on how to have the conversation, as the death of customer discovery is friction.

sections.heading: Episode advice (speaker unidentified)
sections.content: An unidentified speaker advises finding participants who want to opt into research and building a database of customers who are aware of and expect to be contacted for research. They also suggest enabling user researchers to use this database to contact customers more effectively.

sections.heading: Gia Laudi's advice on running customer interviews
sections.content: Gia Laudi suggests working with SparkToro's best customers to learn from them and guide research. She also advises using surveys as a starting point and doubling down with interviews if needed.
